passages.t: At ease in Zion, on beds of ivory
passages.happening:
‘Woe to those at ease in Zion and those secure on Mount Samaria’ (verse 1), the leading men of the foremost nation, to whom Israel comes for help. Go and look at Calneh, Hamath and Gath. Are you better than those kingdoms (verse 2)? They push away the thought of the day of disaster and bring near a reign of violence (verse 3).

‘You lie on beds inlaid with ivory, and lounge upon your couches. You dine on lambs from the flock and calves from the stall’ (verse 4). They make up songs on the harp like David (verse 5). ‘You drink wine by the bowlful and anoint yourselves with the finest oils, but you fail to grieve over the ruin of Joseph’ (verse 6). So they will go into exile first of all, and their feasting and lounging will end (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The chapter opens with the cry of woe, the lament raised over the dead, which Amos speaks over people who are alive and feasting. He names the leaders of both kingdoms, Zion and Samaria.

Verse 2 is debated. Some read it as Amos telling them to look at kingdoms that have already fallen: are you any better? Since Assyria took Calneh and Hamath in the 730s and 720s and Gath fell later, some scholars think the verse was updated after Amos's time. Others read it as the leaders' own boast, or note earlier defeats these cities had suffered. Readers should hold the exact reference loosely.

The details describe real luxury. Excavators at Samaria found hundreds of carved ivory plaques, many once fitted to furniture, from roughly this period. Eating lamb and stall-fattened calves meant eating meat regularly, a rare luxury when most people ate meat only at festivals. Wine drunk from bowls and the finest oils complete the picture. The word for feasting in verse 7 is marzeah, known from texts at Ugarit as a kind of banqueting club, sometimes tied to mourning rites. If so, the irony is sharp: they hold a mourning feast and do not mourn the real ruin of Joseph. The foremost, the finest oils and the first into exile all come from the same Hebrew root.
passages.later: Ahab's ivory house is named in 1 Kings 22:39. Jeremiah uses the same word, marzeah, for a house where there is a funeral meal (Jeremiah 16:5).
passages.hard:
Is Amos condemning wealth, music and feasting as such?

Not as such. The Old Testament elsewhere celebrates feasts, wine, oil and music as good gifts of God: wine ‘that gladdens the heart of man’ (Psalm 104:15). David's music is honored. Amos's target is a particular combination: luxury gained through injustice, enjoyed in complacency, and blind to the suffering of the nation. Some interpreters stress the injustice behind the wealth; others stress the numbness the wealth produced. Both are in the text.

The chapter does not ask whether a person may ever enjoy good things. It asks whether their enjoyment has made them unable to see or feel what is happening to others.
passages.asks: Their sin was not the music but that they did not grieve. Ask what is breaking around you that you have stopped feeling. And ask whether your comforts have made you numb to anyone's ruin.

passages.t: God's oath, and a nation raised up
passages.happening:
The Lord GOD has sworn by himself that he abhors Jacob's pride and detests his fortresses, and he will hand over the city and everything in it (verse 8). If ten men are left in one house, they too will die (verse 9). When a relative comes to carry out the bodies, a survivor will be told to be silent and not to speak the LORD's name (verse 10). The great house and the small house will both be smashed (verse 11).

Do horses gallop on rocky cliffs? Does anyone plow the sea with oxen? Yet they have turned justice into poison and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood (verse 12). They rejoice over Lo-debar and boast that they took Karnaim by their own strength (verse 13). So God will raise up a nation against Israel, which will oppress them ‘from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of the Arabah’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
God swears by himself, the most solemn oath there is, because there is no one greater to swear by. Verses 9 and 10 picture the end of a siege or a plague: a relative comes to dispose of the dead, and a survivor is hushed from even naming the LORD, perhaps for fear that speaking his name would draw more judgment. These notes name the scene and do not dwell on it.

Verse 12 asks absurd questions. Horses do not run on cliffs, and no one plows the sea. Turning justice into poison is just as unnatural. Then come two puns. Lo-debar sounds like nothing, and Karnaim means horns, a sign of strength. These were probably towns east of the Jordan that Jeroboam's armies won back from the Arameans. Israel rejoices over Nothing and boasts that it took Horns by its own strength.

Second Kings says Jeroboam restored Israel's border from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah. Amos turns that very phrase into a threat. The unnamed nation is almost certainly Assyria, which under Tiglath-pileser III, from about 745 BC, began the campaigns that ended with the fall of Samaria in 722 BC.
passages.later: Jeroboam ‘restored the boundary of Israel from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah’ (2 Kings 14:25), the same land Amos says will be oppressed.
passages.asks: Israel boasted that it won by its own strength. Ask what victories you have credited to yourself alone. And ask what pride God might be detesting in the strongholds you have built.
